taurajo_centaur_wind.description:
Scout Ashhoof. Walk with me, I don't like standing where the road can see us.

The Kolkar raiding parties along the eastern approach have grown bolder every week this season, and I can put a date on when it started.

Here's what makes them hard. They strike the road near Far Watch Post, they hit fast, and they're scattered before a proper warband can even form up - never mind ride out.

So we've never fought them. Not once. We've only ever arrived afterward.

And a war you only ever arrive after is one you're losing on a schedule somebody else sets.

I want their numbers thinned while this is still a nuisance.

They ride in small bands out past Far Watch Post. Hit a wagon, hit a scout, vanish.

Thin them and maybe they'll think twice before the next one. Maybe. I'd not promise it.
taurajo_centaur_wind.accept_text: Out past Far Watch Post, along the eastern road.
taurajo_centaur_wind.turn_in_text:
Good. The road's quieter already.

Though I doubt it stays that way for long. Kolkar don't give up territory easy, and I'd think less of them if they did.

taurajo_scout_outposts.description:
Raiders are thinned. Now I want eyes on the Post itself.

Far Watch sits east, right where the road bends toward Durotar.

And I'll be honest with you about why I'm asking rather than sending a runner: it's been eleven days since anything came down that road from them.

That's not alarming on its own. Kelsara runs a quiet post and she's never been one to send word for the sake of it.

It's eleven days in a season where the Kolkar have been doing exactly what they've been doing.

So I'd like somebody to stand in it and look at it. Not ask after it. Stand in it.

Camp Taurajo needs to know the Post is still standing and still ours, and those are two separate questions, and the second one is the one I'm actually asking.
taurajo_scout_outposts.accept_text: Far Watch Post, east where the road bends toward Durotar.
taurajo_scout_outposts.turn_in_text:
Still standing. Good.

Outrider Kelsara's holding that post with fewer grunts than I'd like.

But she's holding it, and I'd rather have her with four than most captains with twenty.

taurajo_outriders_warning.description:
Word's come down from Far Watch and it's worse than raiding.

The Kolkar are massing near Mor'shan Base Camp.

Not gathering. Massing - which is a word I use carefully, and the difference is that a gathering disperses and a mass is waiting for something.

And it's not just raiders out there now. Marauders too.

That's what changed my mind about this whole season. Raiders are opportunists and they go where the wagons are. Marauders don't move for wagons. They move for ground.

So somebody over there has decided the checkpoint is worth taking, and they've started putting the pieces in place to do it.

Break the buildup before it turns into a siege, because once it's a siege we're fighting on their timing again, and I've had a season of that.
taurajo_outriders_warning.accept_text: Near Mor'shan Base Camp, where they're massing.
taurajo_outriders_warning.turn_in_text:
That's a real dent in their numbers.

Warsong Outrider Dask owes you a drink - if orcs drank anything but blackrock ale, which they don't, and I've tried.

taurajo_salvage_wagons.description:
Grainkeeper Yura. Mind the sacks, what's left of them.

I've lost more than one supply wagon to the Kolkar along the eastern road this season. More than one is doing some work in that sentence and I'd rather not give you the figure.

I don't expect the wagons back. A wagon's a wagon and it's gone.

The grain is a different matter.

Because the centaur don't take it. They scatter it - out of the wagon, across the road, and then they ride off and leave it lying there.

They don't eat grain, as far as anyone's established. They do that out of spite, and spite is wasteful, and waste is the thing I actually can't forgive out of all of it.

The sacks are still good. Dirty on the outside, fine underneath.

Bring back what you find, wherever you find it, and the camp eats a little better this week.
taurajo_salvage_wagons.accept_text: Scattered along the eastern road, wherever the wagons were hit.
taurajo_salvage_wagons.turn_in_text:
Dirty, but the grain's fine underneath. It usually is.

The camp thanks you, even if the wagons don't.

taurajo_carvers_materials.description:
Carver Ahonen. Don't move the shavings, they're sorted.

I work centaur horn into totems when I can get it.

I'm aware that's unusual. Plain wood is easier, it's closer, and nobody asks a question about a wooden totem.

I'm not going to tell you why I prefer the horn.

[He keeps working.]

You'll see it eventually. That's not me being difficult, it's that the answer is the finished thing and I'd rather it spoke for itself than have me speak for it badly.

What I need is sun-bleached horn, and only the Marauders carry it. Not the Raiders - theirs is too young and it splits under the knife at the second cut.

The Marauders can occasionally be convinced to part with it.

Clean breaks, if you can manage. A cracked horn is a week of work that ends in a fire.
taurajo_carvers_materials.accept_text: Off the Kolkar marauders - not the raiders, their horn's too young.
taurajo_carvers_materials.turn_in_text:
Good horn. Clean break, no cracks.

This'll carve into something worth having.

Come back in a season and I'll show you what it was for.

taurajo_old_grudges.description:
[The elder does not get up.]

Sit a while.

You're out there fighting the Kolkar - I've watched you come and go three times this week, and you've got the look of someone who's stopped asking why halfway through a job.

You might as well know why they fight us back.

I remember a Barrens before they pressed this far east. Not a story I was told. A thing I walked in, as a young man, when this road went through country that belonged to nobody and we didn't think twice about it.

They remember it too. That's the part nobody at the camp wants said out loud.

I'm not asking you to stop. The raids are real and the wagons are real and my own people are the ones dying on that road.

I'm asking you to carry the whole of it rather than half.

It's easier to swing at a thing you've decided is simple. It is not simple and it never was.
taurajo_old_grudges.accept_text: Sit with Elder Longtread a while.
taurajo_old_grudges.turn_in_text:
Now you understand it isn't just territory.

It's memory, on both sides, and memory doesn't negotiate.

That's worth carrying with you. It'll make you worse company and better at the job.

taurajo_windhoofs_ledger.description:
Hela Windhoof. Quartermaster. I keep this camp's supply ledger and I'd like to show you a page of it.

No - actually, I won't. You'd take it the wrong way and I'd have to explain, and the explaining is the part I'm tired of.

Here's the shape of it.

The losses from Kolkar raids are piling up faster than I can write them off. Not faster than we can replace - faster than I can RECORD. I am behind on my own arithmetic.

That's the figure that matters and nobody above me wants it in those words.

So I want the raiding parties dealt with directly. Properly. Enough to make a real dent and not the token thinning that lets everyone report progress.

I know what I'm asking for and I know it's a lot.

Whichever Kolkar you find - raider, marauder, drudge - it all counts against the same column.
taurajo_windhoofs_ledger.accept_text: Wherever the Kolkar are raiding. Any of them count.
taurajo_windhoofs_ledger.turn_in_text:
The ledger breathes a little easier, and so do I.

I closed three columns this morning that have been open since spring.

Thank you for this.

ratchet_trouble_coast.description:
Customs Officer Prynn. Don't lean on the rail, it's customs property and it's rotten.

I've had reports of pirate activity along Merchant Coast, north of our usual patrol routes.

Now - sailors talk. That's most of what sailors do between jobs and about a third of what they do during one, and if I filed a report on every set of sails somebody swore they saw, Gazlowe would stop reading my reports entirely.

Which is exactly the problem. I get one go at this.

If I take him fishermen's gossip and it's nothing, the next one I bring him - the real one - gets the same shrug.

So I need somebody to actually go and look before I put my name on anything.

Merchant Coast, north of here.

I want colours. Not sails. Colours, and whose they are, from somebody who was standing on the beach.
ratchet_trouble_coast.turn_in_text:
So it's real.

Southsea colours, you said?

Gazlowe is not going to like hearing that, and I am going to enjoy watching him not like it rather more than is professional.

ratchet_cutting_supply_lines.description:
Confirmed is confirmed, so now we move.

And we move now specifically because they haven't finished.

A pirate crew on a beach is a crew. Give them a season and it's a camp - huts, a fire pit, a reason to defend the place rather than sail off it - and then you're not chasing raiders, you're laying siege to neighbours.

I've watched that happen twice on this coast. Once it took four years to undo.

So I want their numbers cut before they dig in and start raiding Ratchet's shipping in earnest, because at the moment they're robbing opportunistically and badly.

The brigands on Merchant Coast. Don't be gentle about it.

Every one you drop is one less problem for this port's trade, and I can put that in a report with a straight face.
ratchet_cutting_supply_lines.accept_text: The Southsea brigands on Merchant Coast.
ratchet_cutting_supply_lines.turn_in_text:
That'll slow them down. Won't stop them.

But it'll slow them, and this week I will take slower.

ratchet_silence_guns.description:
Fuzzek Boomwick. Mind the crates, mind the other crates, don't mind that smell.

The Southsea have dug cannoneers in on Merchant Coast and they are aiming at this harbour.

I want to be straight with you about my motives, because there are two and they're not equal.

The first is Ratchet. That's real. Those are my neighbours and some of them owe me money.

The second is professional and it's the one keeping me up.

That is amateur artillery. I have watched them through a glass and their aim is terrible - genuinely, impressively terrible - and their powder is real.

Those two facts in the same crew is how a harbour loses a warehouse by accident.

I don't like anyone playing with explosives who isn't me, and I'd say that in front of a magistrate.

The cannoneers, on the coast. Gone.
ratchet_silence_guns.accept_text: The Southsea cannoneers dug in on Merchant Coast.
ratchet_silence_guns.turn_in_text:
Fewer amateurs with gunpowder on my coastline.

The harbour's safer, and so is my professional reputation, and I'd struggle to rank those.

ratchet_recovered_cargo.description:
[The fence does not give a name and does not offer one.]

I deal in things that fell off a ship.

That's the whole of the description and it's holding up in every port I've worked, and I'd encourage you not to improve on it.

The Southsea brigands on Merchant Coast are sitting on strongboxes.

Now. Those came off ships. They fell off, in the sense that the ship is at the bottom of something and the box isn't.

Which makes them exactly the sort of goods I handle, and the brigands exactly the sort of previous owner I'm comfortable with.

Bring them to me still locked.

That part isn't negotiable and I'd rather say why than have you wonder: a locked box is a box nobody has to have an opinion about. Open one on that beach and suddenly there's a conversation, and conversations are how people end up in front of a customs officer.

Don't ask what's inside. You wouldn't get a cut anyway.
ratchet_recovered_cargo.accept_text: Off the Southsea brigands on Merchant Coast. Still locked.
ratchet_recovered_cargo.turn_in_text:
Still locked. Exactly how I like them.

Pleasure. Don't make it a habit and don't make it a story.

ratchet_loose_lips.description:
Keep your voice down and don't look at me while I'm talking.

Fintan. I move things through this port that other people would rather were moved quietly, and that means I spend a great deal of time standing near conversations I'm not part of.

I hear things at the docks. Always have. It's the actual asset, more than the boat.

What I've been hearing lately about the Southsea Freebooters has me looking over my shoulder on a street I've walked for nine years.

I want to be clear that I'm not a brave man and I'm not pretending to be one now.

I'm telling you because I've worked out that keeping it to myself is the more dangerous of the two options, and I only worked that out about two days ago.

Ask me what you want to know. Quietly.

And then let me go back to being a man who didn't say anything.
ratchet_loose_lips.accept_text: Talk to Fintan at the docks. Quietly.
ratchet_loose_lips.turn_in_text:
That's everything I know.

And now I'm going to spend a considerable amount of effort pretending I never said any of it.

Good luck out there. Don't come back to this spot.

ratchet_bounty_saltspray.description:
Drask. Bounty hunter, and before you ask - yes, it's a real contract, and no, I'm not telling you who wrote it.

The mark is Captain Saltspray. Southsea officer, holding the Maiden's Dagger on Merchant Coast.

I'll give you my read for nothing, since you're going and I'm not.

Saltspray is the thing holding that operation together. Not because he's good - I've watched him and he isn't, particularly - but because he's the only one on that beach with a rank the others recognise.

Take the head off and the rest scatters. That's not a theory, that's how every crew I've ever hunted has come apart.

It won't be easy. The contract wouldn't pay what it pays if it were, and I've read enough contracts to price a fight off the number.

He didn't make captain by being careless.

He made it by being louder than everyone who was.
ratchet_bounty_saltspray.accept_text: The Maiden's Dagger, on Merchant Coast.
ratchet_bounty_saltspray.turn_in_text:
Saltspray's done.

I'll collect my contract fee, you collect yours. Fair trade and no hard feelings about which of us did the walking.

ratchet_barnacle_bet.description:
Oi! Oi, you - yes. Come here. This is important and it's also a bet.

Barnacle Bill. I missed my ship. Again.

Third time this year and the second time this month, and I want it on the record that twice of those were not my fault and the other one absolutely was.

So rather than sit here being sad about it, I've made a wager with Grizzik over there.

I've bet him that an adventurer passing through could clear out a few Southsea stragglers faster than I can finish this tankard.

[He looks at the tankard.]

I'll grant you I bet against someone who wasn't standing here yet, which Grizzik says is not how a bet works, and I say shows initiative.

Five of them. Any kind.

I've got coin on this. Not much coin. But all of it.
ratchet_barnacle_bet.accept_text: Southsea stragglers, anywhere along the coast. Before the tankard's done.
ratchet_barnacle_bet.turn_in_text:
You actually DID it!

I owe Grizzik a round now - that's how it worked out, he bet on me finishing the drink, and I have been nursing it for an hour out of pure tactics.

I owe you more. Here.

org_word_from_road.description:
Scout Windrider. Orgrimmar's eyes on the Gold Road, which sounds grander than a tent and one spyglass.

My reports have gone quiet.

Not my reports - the ones coming IN to me. That's the distinction and it's the whole problem.

The Gold Road runs from Mor'shan Rampart down toward the Crossroads, and the caravan masters who use it have always been free with information, because a caravan master who tells you about a bad stretch gets told about one in return.

The last few have been thin. Short. Three lines where there used to be a page, from men who like the sound of their own voice.

That's not silence. That's people choosing what to leave out, and I'd like to know what.

Walk the road yourself. The whole length.

See what's slowing them down, and more to the point, see what they've decided not to mention.
org_word_from_road.accept_text: The Gold Road, from Mor'shan Rampart down toward the Crossroads.
org_word_from_road.turn_in_text:
Bandits, you say.

That tracks. That's exactly the thing a caravan master leaves out, because a road with bandits on it is a road people stop hiring him for.

The road's held worse. It needs clearing before it holds much more.

org_keep_road_clear.description:
Bandits confirmed, so now we clear them, and I'd like to be precise about what clearing means.

It does not mean none.

There have been men robbing people on that road since before it was called the Gold Road, and there will be after. Any officer who promises you an empty highway has never held one.

What it means is: few enough that a caravan can take the loss and keep running.

That's the actual line. A caravan master prices in a certain amount of theft the way he prices in a lame ox. When it goes past what he can price, he stops using the road, and then the road dies and takes four towns with it.

We are currently just past that line.

The bandits stage ambushes along the whole length of it.

Cut them back under it. That's the job and it's smaller than it sounds and more important than it looks.
org_keep_road_clear.accept_text: Along the Gold Road, wherever they stage their ambushes.
org_keep_road_clear.turn_in_text:
The road's breathing easier, and so is every caravan master who runs it.

Two of them have already started telling me things again.

org_escalation.description:
This has stopped being banditry and I want to walk you through how I know.

My reports now mention cutthroats. And mounted outriders.

Highwaymen are a trade for men who have run out of other trades. They work alone or in threes, they take what's on top of a wagon, and they do not acquire horses, because a horse eats whether or not you rob anybody.

Cutthroats and outriders in the same operation means somebody is feeding horses through a lean season on the promise of a return.

That's not desperation. That's investment.

Someone is running this with real coordination and real money behind it, and I have no idea who, and that's the part I'd like you to understand before you go out.

Break up whatever this is before it gets any further along.

And if you see anything that looks like an order being given rather than a fight being had - that's what I actually want to hear about.
org_escalation.accept_text: Along the Gold Road. The organised ones, not the stragglers.
org_escalation.turn_in_text:
Nine down, and no sign of who's running them. Yet.

That's a problem for another day and it is going to be a large one.

Today, the road's clear.

org_feathers_fury.description:
Rethok. Hunter.

I want harpy feathers. Witchwing, out of the Dry Hills.

[He waits to see if you'll ask.]

I collect them. That's as much as I generally say and it's as much as most people want, and I've found that the ones who push tend to be the ones I'd rather not sell to.

I'll tell you this much, because you're the one going out there and it's useful.

The feathers hum. Not all of them - maybe one in six, and it's never the biggest or the brightest, and I have never worked out what makes the difference.

The ones that hum are the ones worth something to the right buyer, and no, I'm not telling you who.

They're nasty things, the Witchwing. Out in the hills proper, not the fringe.

Bring me what you get and I'll sort them myself.
org_feathers_fury.accept_text: Off the Witchwing harpies out in the Dry Hills.
org_feathers_fury.turn_in_text:
Good feathers. And still humming with a little magic.

Exactly what I needed. I'll not say for what.

org_slayers_ring.description:
Now the part that isn't trade.

The Witchwing slayers are not ordinary harpies and I'd not send you at them for feathers.

They're Serena Bloodfeather's lieutenants. You'll know them by the rings they carry - every one of them, the same make, which tells you they were given and not found.

That's a chain of command. Out here, among harpies, somebody sat down and decided who answers to whom and gave out tokens to prove it.

I've hunted in these hills eighteen years and I have never seen harpies do that before her.

So: the slayers first, and Serena after. Not the other way round.

Kill her with the slayers alive and the hills have four leaders inside a month, and I'd be starting again against people I've not learned yet.

Take the rings off them. I want to lay them out and count.
org_slayers_ring.accept_text: The Witchwing slayers in the Dry Hills. They carry the rings.
org_slayers_ring.turn_in_text:
Four rings, four slayers.

Serena's down to just herself now.

That's exactly where I want her, and it took two years to get there.

org_serenas_head.description:
She's alone now. So here's the last of it, and I'll tell it straight because she's earned that much from somebody.

Serena Bloodfeather attacks Horde caravans. She has for years. People have died on that road because of her and I'm not going to soften it.

She does it out of grief.

Her sister was killed - by Rexxar, if you want the name, and I'd rather you had it than a rumour. And Serena has spent every season since turning that into other people's funerals.

She won't stop. Grief doesn't stop just because everyone you sent ahead of you is dead, and she sent the slayers out precisely so she wouldn't have to be the one standing there.

End it.

She deserves better than to keep bleeding for a sister who isn't coming back.

And the caravans deserve to stop paying for it. Both of those are true at once and I've stopped trying to put one first.
org_serenas_head.accept_text: In the Dry Hills. She's alone now.
org_serenas_head.turn_in_text:
It's done.

I won't pretend that's a clean kind of victory, and I'd think less of you if you did.

But the road's safer. Sometimes that has to be enough, and most days out here it is.

nb_toll_collectors.description:
Hargak. Waystation's mine, which means the road's my problem whether or not anyone's written that down.

The Gold Road is the only honest thing in the Northern Barrens. Everything else out here is a claim, a rumour or a goblin, and the road just goes where it says it goes.

Someone's started charging for it.

Bandits at the bends. They're polite for exactly one sentence - I've heard it, it's a good sentence, somebody taught it to them - and then every wagon that can't pay goes on lighter.

They wear their coats turned the wrong way round so you can't tell who they are under them.

I can tell. I've been looking at the backs of those coats for a season.

Thin them out along the bends, and bring me whatever they're carrying.

I've run out of patience in the specific way where you don't get it back.
nb_toll_collectors.accept_text: At the bends along the Gold Road. Their coats are on the wrong way round.
nb_toll_collectors.turn_in_text:
Fewer coats, more wagons. That's the arithmetic I like.

Here. The waystation's thanks.

nb_the_highwaymans_ledger.description:
Bandits keep books.

I find that funny and I find it useful, and I've had three people tell me I shouldn't find it both.

Every one of them carries a page. Stained, folded over about nine times, and it says who paid, who didn't, and which wagons are worth the trouble.

That last column is the one that keeps me up. Somebody is making judgements out there about which drivers are worth stopping, and the judgements are good ones.

Collect enough pages and you can read the route they plan to work next.

Look in the coat linings. They think nobody checks there, and they're right about nearly everybody.

Bring me a stack, not one. One page is a day. A stack is a plan.
nb_the_highwaymans_ledger.accept_text: Off the road bandits at the bends. Check the coat linings.
nb_the_highwaymans_ledger.turn_in_text:
Mm.

They're going to hit the coast road next.

I'd better tell someone with a spear. Take this.

nb_cutthroats_on_the_road.description:
The pages named a crew, and it isn't the one I thought I was fighting.

Cutthroats on foot. Outriders on beasts. Working the stretch between the oasis fork and the coast, together, on a rotation.

These are not toll collectors.

I want that distinction understood, because I've spent a season being almost relieved that the road had bandits who asked first. A toll collector wants you to come back next month with money.

These ones don't ask.

The cutthroats move in pairs and the outriders cover them from a distance, which is a soldier's arrangement and not a bandit's, and I've stopped wondering where they learned it.

Take the outriders' bows out of it first if you can manage the order.

They hurt considerably more than they look like they should.
nb_cutthroats_on_the_road.accept_text: Between the oasis fork and the coast. Outriders first if you can.
nb_cutthroats_on_the_road.turn_in_text:
The road's quiet. First time in a season.

You've earned more than I can pay, but this is what I have.

nb_wreckers_beach.description:
Kizzle. Beachmaster, which is a title I gave myself and have successfully defended.

The Merchant Coast is this whole region's loading dock. Everything that comes into the Barrens by water comes in over my planks, and I would like that sentence to keep being true.

Every crab in the bay has decided it owns the pier.

Tide-Wreckers. Big, red, sulky, and they pry the planks off cargo crates - off the crates, bro, not out of them - and drag the planks out to sea, and nobody sees the planks or the crab again.

I have no idea what they're doing with them. I've got a theory involving a very large nest and I've stopped sharing it.

I asked nicely. I did the whole thing, I stood on the beach, I asked.

Now I'm asking differently.

They hide in the surf. Crack a few and the rest will remember they've got other places to be.
nb_wreckers_beach.accept_text: In the surf along the pier. Big, red, sulky.
nb_wreckers_beach.turn_in_text:
Listen to that, bro. Nothing! Not one claw!

Take this, with the beachmaster's gratitude.

nb_salvage_rights.description:
Second problem, and this one's got a legal dimension I'd like to walk you through carefully.

Southsea Brigands have been dragging cargo crates up the beach and prying them open.

Now. Anything they've already opened is theirs, as a practical matter, because I am not going door to door on a pirate beach with an inventory.

But anything they HAVEN'T opened yet is still, strictly speaking, the Merchants' property.

I want to be clear that my definition of 'strictly speaking' has been reviewed by nobody and has never once lost an argument.

So go get the unopened ones.

And don't open them. I know what's in them.

Don't ask how.
nb_salvage_rights.accept_text: Up the beach, where the Southsea crews have dragged them. The unopened ones.
nb_salvage_rights.turn_in_text:
These are mine! Er. The Merchants'.

Same thing, really.

Take this for your trouble.

nb_silence_the_cannons.description:
Right, this one's urgent and I'd like to get through it quickly for reasons that will become obvious.

The Southsea crews have mounted cannons on the cliffs. Three of them. They're using them for target practice on anything that floats, which out here means my inbound shipping and the occasional confused whale.

I have a written guarantee - Ratchet-built, properly stamped - that this pier is 'definitely not in range'.

It is definitely in range.

I've had the guarantee out twice this week and read it in the direction of the cliffs and it has not helped.

Cannoneers stand behind the brigands. So cut through the brigands.

And whatever else you do up there - don't stand in a line. They've got nothing to aim at but lines.
nb_silence_the_cannons.accept_text: Up on the cliffs above the coast. Cut through the brigands to reach the guns.
nb_silence_the_cannons.turn_in_text:
Quiet again! Well. 'Quiet' for a harbour.

Here, take this. It's cleaner than it looks.

nb_captain_saltspray.description:
Last one, and then you and I are going to sit on a crate and not talk about pirates.

Captain Saltspray runs the Southsea crew.

He is not good at it. I want that on the record because everyone who hears the word 'captain' assumes competence, and I've watched this man run a beach for two years.

He's loud. That's the whole of his gift. And loud is enough, because the cannoneers are brave when he's shouting and ordinary when he isn't, and I've seen the exact moment it switches over.

So here's your fight: he shows himself when his crew is winning.

Make them stop winning.

Then make him regret showing himself.
nb_captain_saltspray.accept_text: On the beach with his crew. He only shows himself when they're winning.
nb_captain_saltspray.turn_in_text:
The captain's down and the beach is ours again.

Come back in a week. There'll be a drink with your name on it.

nb_hounds_of_the_oasis.description:
Mahri. Keep your voice down near the water - sound carries off it further than you'd think, and I've learned that the expensive way.

The Stagnant Oasis hasn't been fit to drink from in years. Everyone knows that. It still draws every wanderer on the plains, because people will walk toward water they've been told is bad on the grounds that somebody must have been exaggerating.

Lately it draws something else.

Dervish hounds. Lean, mange-ridden things the Kolkar dervishes breed and set loose out here - not to guard anything. To be loose.

They circle first and bite after, and the circling is the part that gets people, because it goes on long enough that you start thinking about something else.

Keep your back to something solid. A cliff, a tent, anything.

I want them gone before they work out what a campfire is for.
nb_hounds_of_the_oasis.accept_text: Around the Stagnant Oasis. Keep your back to something solid.
nb_hounds_of_the_oasis.turn_in_text:
They've stopped howling.

I never realised how much of the night they were filling until it wasn't.

Take this.

nb_curved_blades.description:
Now something stranger, and I'd like you to collect carefully rather than quickly.

The Kolkar dervishes fight with curved blades, and they sharpen them on the same stones they pray at. Same stones. I watched that for a month before I believed what I was looking at.

My scouts want a handful of those blades. Not to use - to read.

The edges carry marks. Every dervish grinds a little differently and every trainer passes his grind down, so a blade will tell you who taught the man holding it, and who taught him.

That's a family tree, out here, where nobody writes anything down.

Cut them off the bodies. Don't clean them - the grit on them is half the reading.

Bring me enough to lay side by side and I'll show you what the marks mean.
nb_curved_blades.accept_text: Off the Kolkar dervishes at the oasis. Don't clean them.
nb_curved_blades.turn_in_text:
These are from the same forge. All of them.

There's a smith feeding the whole camp, and that's a thing we didn't know this morning.

Take this.

nb_stormcallers.description:
There's a band of Kolkar stormcallers at the far side of the oasis, and they are drawing lightning out of a sky that has not seen rain in months.

It isn't working. I'd like to lead with that so you go in at the right level of alarm.

Whatever they're calling, it isn't coming. I've watched eleven days of it and the most they've managed is to make the air taste like a struck anvil.

It's still giving every creature within a mile a headache, mine included, and I have begun losing the thread of sentences halfway through them, which in a scout is not a joke.

They stay together in the middle and the dervishes ring them.

Break the ring, then the casters.

And don't stand in the lightning. I mean that literally - people have taken it as a figure of speech.
nb_stormcallers.accept_text: Far side of the oasis. Break the dervish ring, then the casters.
nb_stormcallers.turn_in_text:
The sky is quiet. Wonderful.

I can hear the wind again. I'd forgotten it had a sound of its own.

Take this, with the camp's thanks.

nb_verog_the_dervish.description:
Verog leads them, and I've had longer than I'd like to work out what he actually is.

Fast. Patient. And quick to be offended - which sounds like a weakness and is the opposite.

That's why the Kolkar put him here. A man who can be goaded is the finest bait a warband could ask for, because every hero who comes through this oasis thinks the temper is the way in.

They get him angry. He spins. They die in the spin.

I have buried four of those heroes and I'd rather not make it five.

So: the dervishes around him first. You want him alone, and you want the room empty when it turns.

He spins when he's angry and he is always angry.

Wait for the spin to wind down. Then hit him.
nb_verog_the_dervish.accept_text: At the heart of the oasis. Clear the dervishes round him first.
nb_verog_the_dervish.turn_in_text:
Verog's dead.

I never thought I'd see that, and I've been here long enough to have stopped saying things like that out loud.

Take this, and let me be the first to buy you a drink.

nb_raiders_at_the_gate.description:
Outrider Kelsara. Far Watch holds the eastern road and the Kolkar know exactly what that means, which is more than I can say for half of Orgrimmar.

Every dawn another band rides up the headland, circles the tower, tests the palisade and goes.

That's not an attack. That's a survey.

I've counted forty since the last full moon. Forty - I kept the tally on the gatepost until somebody painted over it, and then I kept it in a book.

And somewhere in there I stopped counting them as people and started counting them as a number going up, and I've noticed that about myself and I haven't decided what to do with it.

They test the weak spots.

There aren't any. Convince them of that with a spear.
nb_raiders_at_the_gate.accept_text: On the headland below the tower, at the palisade.
nb_raiders_at_the_gate.turn_in_text:
Nothing at the palisade for an hour now. Almost suspicious.

Take this and don't question luck.

nb_war_pennants.description:
Every Kolkar warband carries a pennant. A strip of dyed hide on a stick, and it tells the others who's giving orders.

Take enough of them off the field and the bands lose their way - not permanently, they're not fools, but long enough to matter.

That's the practical reason and it's a good one.

Here's the real one. I have been reading the same colours at the same hour every single morning for six weeks. Same order, same gap between them, same band on the left.

I can tell you what time it is by which pennant is on the headland and that is not a skill a person should have.

Bring them in.

And don't burn them. I want to read them side by side first, because I've a suspicion about those colours and I'd like to be wrong.
nb_war_pennants.accept_text: Off the Kolkar warbands on the headland. Don't burn them.
nb_war_pennants.turn_in_text:
The colours match three different bands.

They've united. That's bad.

Take this, and be quick going back out.

nb_scoutriders_on_the_headland.description:
Two problems and they're the same problem, which took me longer to work out than I'll admit in writing.

Kolkar scoutriders ride the headland every night, measuring the tower's blind spots.

I haven't got blind spots. I've walked that ground with a lantern at every hour there is, and I'd back this tower's sight-lines against anything on the plain.

What I have got is drudges stealing off the supply line while the scouts are being watched.

That's the arrangement. The scouts aren't surveying anything - they're being looked at, on purpose, every night, so that nobody on this wall is looking the other way.

It worked for a month.

Scoutriders on beasts, drudges on foot.

Cut the drudges first. They're slow, and the scouts will come down to rescue them - which is the one thing about this whole arrangement that I actually respect.
nb_scoutriders_on_the_headland.accept_text: On the headland after dark. Drudges first - the scouts will come to them.
nb_scoutriders_on_the_headland.turn_in_text:
The headland's quiet again.

You've earned this, and a place in my orders.

nb_kragg_the_wall_breaker.description:
Kragg is a warbrand chief who has never met a palisade he didn't want to test.

He rides a hide-clad warbeast and he brings a ram, and he has brought that ram to four different walls that I know of, and three of those walls are gone.

This one has stood ten years.

He's decided that's too long. I don't know how I know that and I'm certain of it anyway - you watch a thing circle your wall enough times and you learn what it's thinking.

He comes at dusk, usually.

Warbrands first. Then him.

And I'll be plain with you about the stakes rather than making you guess: if he reaches this wall with that ram, every one of us behind it finds out together what happens next.
nb_kragg_the_wall_breaker.accept_text: Below the palisade at dusk. Warbrands first, then him.
nb_kragg_the_wall_breaker.turn_in_text:
Kragg's down. The wall holds.

I'll raise a drink and a banner, in that order.

Take this - the Post's thanks.

nb_slugs_in_the_reeds.description:
Dugmok. Warden of the fens, which used to be the quietest posting in the Barrens and no longer is.

The Slug Fens were only ever slow, wet and quiet. That's the whole of what this place was. You could walk the causeway with your eyes shut and the worst thing that happened was your boots.

Then the slugs got big.

I don't know why. Nobody does, and I've asked three shaman and a goblin, and the goblin wanted paying.

Pale, fat, and bigger than a dog now, and they're creeping across the causeway at night.

My wardens keep that causeway open. That's the job and it's the only job.

Because nobody wants to be the one who explains why a caravan went in and the cargo came out as soup.

Cut them back off it. If they wriggle, hit harder.
nb_slugs_in_the_reeds.accept_text: Along the causeway through the fens.
nb_slugs_in_the_reeds.turn_in_text:
Quiet. Thick, wet, honest quiet.

Thank you. Take this, with the fen's thanks.

nb_venom_glands.description:
Now a thing I want and will not fetch myself, and I'd rather say that plainly than dress it up as delegation.

The fen slugs carry a venom gland in the back. Green sac, about the size of a fist on the big ones.

Cured right, it makes a first-rate poison. I know how. My mother knew how and her hands were steadier than mine have been for about four years.

So: cut them out whole.

Whole, hear me. Don't pop them.

If one goes while you're carrying it we'll be burying a tauren, and the ceremony is long and I'd be at it instead of here.

The next caravan through this causeway is going to want every advantage it can carry.
nb_venom_glands.accept_text: Off the fen slugs along the causeway. Cut them out whole.
nb_venom_glands.turn_in_text:
Good clean glands. Not a mark on them.

I'll make something up for the next caravan. Take this.

nb_peat_hearts.description:
Deep in the fens the peat has started to move.

I'd like a moment of credit for how calmly I said that, because it took me a season to be able to.

Peat shamblers. Mud, root, and old bog-oak that's been down there since before the Horde crossed the sea, and they shuffle the causeway at night.

They don't hunt. They go up and down it, and anything on the causeway while they're doing that is simply in the way.

At the heart of each one there's a core, and it's warm.

Not warm the way a body is. Warm the way a banked fire is, hours after, and it does not go out when you take it out of the thing.

I can burn those through a whole cold winter and my wardens can stop choosing between firewood and sleep.

You'll have to break them for it. Hit the middle. It's a lump about the size of your fist.
nb_peat_hearts.accept_text: The deep fen, off the causeway at night. Hit the middle.
nb_peat_hearts.turn_in_text:
Ha! Warm already.

You're a wonder. Take this.

nb_old_mire_maw.description:
There's something at the bottom of the deep fen, and I've been three years not asking you about it.

Old Mire-Maw. A crocolisk older than the causeway and wider than a wagon - and I mean the causeway itself, which my grandfather's people laid, so take that how you like.

I've lost three wardens to it.

I knew all three. I sent all three. The first one was an accident, the second was bad luck, and the third was me still calling it bad luck.

That's enough. That's the whole of my reasoning and I'm not going to make it sound more strategic than it is.

It hides in the deep pools at the end of the causeway.

Don't stand in the water. Don't stand near the water.

If you can manage it, don't stand.
nb_old_mire_maw.accept_text: The deep pools at the end of the causeway.
nb_old_mire_maw.turn_in_text:
Mire-Maw's dead.

I never thought I'd say it, and I've practised saying it, which tells you something.

Come back and I'll carve you something out of its tooth.

nb_rig_crews.description:
Keep off the skyline coming up to the shack. Nix. Sludge inspector, which is a title I made up, for a job nobody's hiring.

I worked for the Venture Company. Years. Good years, honestly - I'm not going to pretend I was miserable, because the lie would show.

Then I found out what they were doing down in the fen.

Now I sit in a rusted shack and count crews, which is a career trajectory I'd advise against.

They're drilling day and night. The ground is bleeding black and it's reaching the water, and I've been watching the edge of the stain move for eleven months.

I want the crews gone.

And - this is the part I need you to hear properly - preferably without anyone I like standing in the way.

I know most of them. I trained some of them. I'm asking anyway, which is the whole of what I've got to give this fen.

The drillers are the loud ones. Stop the noise and the guards come out, and the guards are quieter and nastier.
nb_rig_crews.accept_text: At the rig, down in the fen. The drillers are the loud ones.
nb_rig_crews.turn_in_text:
Quiet! Real quiet.

The fen's got a pulse again.

Take this, from a man who knows exactly what it's worth.

nb_pressure_gauges.description:
Every rig has a gauge. Every gauge tells a story, and I can read this particular story faster than anyone alive, which is the one advantage I've got left from that job.

How hard they're drilling. How deep. And how close this whole fen is to going up.

That last number is the one I need, and I can't get it with a glass from a hill.

The pumpjack guards keep them on a chain at the belt.

So cut the chain.

Don't cut the guard's friends - that's not squeamishness, it's that they fight back as a unit and a chain is a two-second job if nobody's shouting yet.

I used to ask nicely for readings. I had a clipboard and everything.

I've lost the nerve for it, and I'd rather tell you that than have you find out when I hesitate.
nb_pressure_gauges.accept_text: Off the pumpjack guards at the rig. They keep them on a belt chain.
nb_pressure_gauges.turn_in_text:
Ha. Look at that needle.

They're drilling too deep. It's going to blow.

Take this and keep your distance.

nb_sludge_samples.description:
Where the oil's pooled, the sludge has started to move.

Sludge elementals. Black, sticky, and very angry, and I want to be careful about that last word because I don't think it's a metaphor.

Something down there got poured into enough of itself to start having opinions.

I want samples. Not for the fen - the fen is past arguments. For the Company.

Because the Board will say the drilling is clean right up until somebody puts a jar on the table, and I have sat in those rooms and watched exactly that happen over something smaller.

Take the samples from the middle of them. That's where it's purest and it's also where they are, so I'm aware of what I'm asking.

They leave a slick behind. Careful on it.

The goop does not come off. Ever. I've still got some.
nb_sludge_samples.accept_text: Off the sludge elementals where the oil's pooled. Take it from the middle.
nb_sludge_samples.turn_in_text:
Look at that. Pure, black, and very illegal.

They won't be able to deny this one.

Take this.

nb_supervisor_lugwizzle.description:
Lugwizzle runs the rig.

He screams. He throws wrenches - at people, at machines, at the fen generally when there's nobody closer. And he signs every order that comes off that platform.

That last one is why we're talking.

I've watched a lot of goblins run a lot of operations, and most of them delegate the signing because signing is how you end up in front of a Board. He doesn't. Everything that happens down there happens because he put his name to it that morning.

Which means if he stops, the rig stops.

And if the rig stops, the fen heals. Slowly. Probably not in my lifetime, and I've made peace with the arithmetic of that.

Here's the map to the pumphouse. I drew it from memory and the memory's good.

He's usually in there, shouting.

He throws oil. Don't stand in it.
nb_supervisor_lugwizzle.accept_text: The pumphouse at the rig. He's usually inside, shouting.
nb_supervisor_lugwizzle.turn_in_text:
Lugwizzle's down and the rig's quiet.

Take this. I owe you considerably more than I'll ever have.

nb_engineer_whirleygig.description:
With Lugwizzle gone, the engineer is panicking, and a panicking engineer is a different kind of problem from an angry supervisor.

Whirleygig is the one who actually made those drillers work. Lugwizzle signed the orders; Whirleygig made the thing in the order exist, which is a distinction the Company has never once paid for correctly.

He's building something in the back of the shop. Large. Noisy. He's been at it since the pumphouse went quiet and he hasn't come out.

It is going to explode.

I know I say that a lot. I've said it about a pump, a cart and a kettle this year alone.

I was right about all three.

He's got turrets up. Kill the guards, then him.

And whatever you do, don't be standing near him when he trips the switch - because he will trip it, the moment he decides he's losing.
nb_engineer_whirleygig.accept_text: The back of the rig's workshop. Guards first, then him.
nb_engineer_whirleygig.turn_in_text:
The thing's dead, the engineer's dead, and this fen will heal in time.

Take this. It's the last of what I own that's worth giving.

nb_claim_jumpers.description:
Gruda. Surveyor. And before you ask - yes, I have the paperwork.

The Boulder Lode was a Horde claim. Filed, stamped, witnessed by two people who are still alive and will still say so.

Then the Venture Company moved in, and now their miners swing picks on my walls and their overseers shout in my tunnels.

The paperwork is not helping.

I've had it out at the mine mouth. I've read the relevant line aloud to a goblin holding a clipboard, and he wrote something down, and nothing happened, and I am fairly sure what he wrote down was my name.

So we move to the part of the dispute where the paperwork stays in my pack.

Go in and clear the miners out of the lower galleries.

They're not soldiers. I'd like that said before you go, because it changes nothing and it's still true.

They'll hit you with a pick all the same.
nb_claim_jumpers.accept_text: The lower galleries of the Boulder Lode.
nb_claim_jumpers.turn_in_text:
The lower galleries are ours again. I can hear the dust settling.

Take this.

nb_heart_of_the_vein.description:
Now something I can only get from inside, and it's the thing I actually came out here for.

The elementals in that mine are made of the same rock as the walls. Same stone, same seams - and the walls are laced with crystal all the way through.

So they carry the vein in them. Break one open and you're holding a core sample that nobody had to cut.

If I can read those, I can tell you how much the Company has already taken out of my claim. Not estimate. Tell you, to within a season.

That's a number I can put in front of somebody in Orgrimmar who outranks a clipboard.

Break them open. You'll find a glowing core in each one.

Bring me a handful - a single core is a spot, a row of them is a vein, and I need the vein.
nb_heart_of_the_vein.accept_text: Off the rock elementals in the mine's galleries.
nb_heart_of_the_vein.turn_in_text:
The vein's rich. Richer than they ever let on.

And they've taken nearly half of it.

Take this, with my thanks.

nb_sprites_in_the_seams.description:
The ore sprites are small, bright and mean, in that order and with no gaps between.

They live in the crystal seams. They bite anything that gets close, which in a working mine is everything, constantly - and I'd have written them off as vermin except for one thing.

They only live in the rich seams.

Never the poor ones. Not once, in six months of looking, and I was looking specifically to disprove it.

So a sprite is an assay with legs, and I'd like some chips off them for my table.

Quick and glowing, and they pause to sparkle - every one of them, every time. Hit them in the pause. They cannot help it and I've stopped feeling clever about it.

And don't breathe their dust. I did, once, and I tasted copper for a week.
nb_sprites_in_the_seams.accept_text: In the crystal seams of the mine. Hit them while they pause to sparkle.
nb_sprites_in_the_seams.turn_in_text:
Beautiful. And they test out rich, too, which confirms the whole theory.

Take this, with the claim's thanks.

nb_prospector_delvik.description:
[She takes a while over this one.]

Delvik was my partner.

Twenty-two years. We filed the Boulder Lode together, both names on the stamp, and his hand is on half of the original survey.

He sold the claim's map to the Venture Company. For a promise and a bag of silver, and I've had a long time to decide which half of that insults me more.

Now he's in a side adit with a rifle and a bad conscience, and he hasn't come out, and the Company hasn't come to get him either - which tells you precisely what the promise was worth.

I'd like him to explain himself. If that's possible.

If it isn't, it won't be a surprise and I'd ask you not to soften it for me afterward.

Side adit off the middle gallery, behind the rubble pile.

He shoots first. Tinkerers keep him company. Clear them and you've done most of the work.
nb_prospector_delvik.accept_text: A side adit off the middle gallery, behind the rubble.
nb_prospector_delvik.turn_in_text:
So he did get what he deserved.

I'd have wished him a quieter end. I'm not sorry, though, and I've stopped waiting to be.

Take this.

nb_foreman_grills.description:
Top of the mine, round a vein of blue crystal, Foreman Grills runs the Company's crew.

Iron hat. Bullhorn. And, in his own estimation, the cleverest man ever to hold a pick.

I've met him. He told me that - not as a boast, as background, the way you'd mention where you were born.

He is the loudest man ever to hold a pick. That I'll grant him without argument.

But he's been working that blue seam for four months and he's taking it out in the wrong order, and anybody who'd actually read a vein would know that, and nobody up there will tell him.

That's how the whole claim ends up ruined even if we win.

He's at the top, in the crystal chamber. Overseers hold the way up.

Take them out and he's alone - if you can call a man with a bullhorn alone.
nb_foreman_grills.accept_text: The crystal chamber at the top of the mine. Overseers hold the way up.
nb_foreman_grills.turn_in_text:
Grills is dead, the claim's ours, and the vein will outlast every one of us.

Take this, with the claim's honour.

nb_siege_lines.description:
Outrider Dask. Mind the guy-ropes, half this camp is held up by rope and optimism.

Mor'shan Base Camp sits under the Rampart like a thorn in the Kaldorei's side. That's not me being poetic - that is the entire strategic purpose of this camp and it was explained to me in those words.

So the Kolkar warbrands surround it.

And I don't blame them. I'd attack too. If somebody put a camp under my hill specifically to be a thorn, I would go and remove the thorn, and I'd do it before breakfast.

I've said that out loud to my own officers and it did not go well.

What I'd like is simpler than a war: get them off the supply road.

Warbrands are tough, loud, and always in a group of four. Break one group and the rest will think twice.

Don't think twice yourself.
nb_siege_lines.accept_text: On the supply road below Mor'shan. They move in fours.
nb_siege_lines.turn_in_text:
The supply road's clear! Well. Clearer.

Take this, from a grateful outrider.

nb_break_the_scouts.description:
Scoutriders work the hills above this camp and report every movement to the Rampart.

I don't mind being watched. I want to be clear about that because the last person I sent up there went in angry about the principle and came back with an arrow in him.

Watching is fair. We watch them. Everyone out here watches everyone and nobody has ever died of it.

I mind being shot at, which they do for sport, from a range where it can't possibly be about the camp.

That's the bit that's got nothing to do with the war.

They shoot from distance and run.

Chase the slow ones. The fast ones will come back on their own - they always do, they can't stand not knowing how it finished.
nb_break_the_scouts.accept_text: The hills above the base camp. Chase the slow ones.
nb_break_the_scouts.turn_in_text:
They've stopped watching. Good.

I can have a quiet breakfast for once.

Take this.

nb_scout_captain_vrek.description:
Vrek commands the Rampart-watchers. He's the one who tells the Kaldorei when to shoot.

That's the whole of his function and it is worth more to them than any four warbands - a hundred riders can see a thing, but somebody has to decide it matters and say so, and that somebody is him.

He rides with a hawk. Sharp-eyed, trained, and between the pair of them there is nothing on this plain they haven't looked at.

I want him blind. Preferably permanently, and I'm aware of how that's phrased.

He hides among the scoutriders, which is good sense and makes the fight awkward.

If you can reach him, he's weak - he's a pair of eyes, not a warrior.

If he reaches you, you're not.
nb_scout_captain_vrek.accept_text: Among the scoutriders in the hills. He hides in the middle of them.
nb_scout_captain_vrek.turn_in_text:
Vrek's down. The Rampart can't see us for a day or two.

That may be all we need.

Take this.

nb_pickets_past_the_wall.description:
Captain Korvash. Stand behind the stone when you're talking to me - they've got archers on those cliffs with nothing else to do.

The Rampart is the Horde's wall against the Kaldorei, and I'll tell you the thing nobody puts in a dispatch: it's a wall with a very thin side.

That strip just north of the gate is the thin side.

Sentinel pickets hold it. Archers cover them from the cliffs. And between them they shoot anything that comes within a hundred paces of our own gate, which means we are not holding a wall, we are living behind one.

I've been polite about this for two seasons. I've sent letters.

I'm done being polite.

Clear the strip.

The pickets hold the line and the archers cover them, so take the archers first if you can manage it.

Don't be proud about the order. Proud is how the last two went.
nb_pickets_past_the_wall.accept_text: The strip just north of the Rampart gate. Archers first if you can.
nb_pickets_past_the_wall.turn_in_text:
The strip's quiet. For now.

They'll send more. They always send more.

Take this.

nb_signal_horns.description:
Every sentinel picket out there carries a signal horn.

One blast and the whole forest answers. Not a patrol - the forest. I've heard it once, from this gate, and I've organised two seasons of orders around never hearing it again.

I want them off the field before the Kaldorei work out how thin this Rampart actually is.

Because that's the real position, and I'd rather you knew it going out. We're not holding them back. We're holding a line they have not yet decided to test properly, and a horn is how the deciding would start.

Cut them off the belts. Quick, before they get them up.

Bring them to me. I want to see them in a pile - and I want to count them, because the count is the only measure I've got of how much time we just bought.
nb_signal_horns.accept_text: Off the sentinel pickets north of the gate. Cut them off the belt before they sound.
nb_signal_horns.turn_in_text:
Five horns. Five fewer calls for help.

That's a good day, and I don't get many.

Take this.

nb_moonspeakers.description:
Behind the pickets stand the moonspeakers.

Priestesses. They call light down on anyone who falls, and they are the reason I have killed the same sentinel three times.

I want you to sit with that a moment, because it took me most of a season to understand what it was doing to my own people.

My grunts stopped believing their work counted. You put a picket down, you see her stand up, and the next time you go in a little slower - not out of fear, out of the sense that nothing you do out there stays done.

That's what's actually holding this line. Not the archers.

Take them out and it breaks.

They stand at the back, glowing, which is either confidence or a uniform and I've never settled it.

Close on them fast. They run if you give them the time to decide to.
nb_moonspeakers.accept_text: Behind the picket line, north of the gate. They stand at the back.
nb_moonspeakers.turn_in_text:
The line's breaking. That's what we've been waiting for.

Take this, with the Rampart's thanks.

nb_warden_ilthae.description:
Their commander at this wall is Warden Ilthae.

Old. Steady. Silver-haired, and she has not lost a skirmish in twenty years, which I know because I've been on the wrong end of four of them and I keep a record.

I respect her. I'd like that said once, plainly, and then I'd like it not to come up again.

She does not waste her people. Every time I have pushed at that strip she has given me exactly enough ground to make the push expensive and not one step more, and she has never once chased me when chasing would have cost her.

That is a better officer than I am. I've thought about it enough.

I'd still like her dead, because she is the thing standing between the Horde and this road, and respect was never the same as agreement.

She's got a glaive, a bad temper and no fear at all.

Don't fight her in the open. Don't fight her at all, if you can avoid it.

But you can't.
nb_warden_ilthae.accept_text: At the Rampart line, behind the pickets.
nb_warden_ilthae.turn_in_text:
Ilthae's dead. The strip is ours.

Take this, and may this wall hold a little longer than she thought it would.

nb_feathers_on_the_wind.description:
Zan'ula. Keep walking while we talk, I don't stand still in these hills and neither should you.

The Dry Hills belong to the Witchwings. That's not me conceding anything - it's a tracker's statement of fact, and the sooner you accept it the longer you live up here.

They're harpies, and they've learned a few tricks from somewhere dark. I've tracked harpies my whole life. These ones do things the others don't, and I've not found who taught them.

I track them for a living and I'd like fewer of them to track.

They fly low over the ridges and strike from behind. Always behind. Every single time, and knowing it doesn't help as much as you'd hope.

Keep your back to a hill and you'll be fine.
nb_feathers_on_the_wind.accept_text: Over the ridges of the Dry Hills. Keep your back to a hill.
nb_feathers_on_the_wind.turn_in_text:
Good. Quiet in the hills.

For a day or so. Take this.

nb_hexed_totems.description:
The windcallers carve hex-totems and hang them up in the high rocks.

I don't know what they do.

I want to be honest about that rather than invent a reason, because every tracker I've met who invented a reason ended up believing it.

Here's what I've got. I camp near them and I dream badly. Not nightmares - I'd take nightmares, I've had those since I was a girl. Bad in the sense that I wake up having decided things.

Twice I've woken up with a plan I didn't make, and both plans involved going further into those hills.

So I'd like them down.

Pull them off the windcallers.

And don't look at them for long. I'm aware of how that sounds coming from a woman who just admitted she doesn't know what they do.
nb_hexed_totems.accept_text: Off the Witchwing windcallers in the high rocks.
nb_hexed_totems.turn_in_text:
Mm. They feel wrong even in a bag.

I'll burn them tonight. Thank you.

Take this.

nb_hillcrest_stalkers.description:
Something else has been working the trail between the hills, and it isn't harpies.

Hillcrest stalkers. Patient, grey, and cunning in the specific way that makes a hunter uneasy - they don't ambush where the ground is good for ambushing. They ambush where you stop looking.

I've watched one let a traveller pass under it twice before taking him on the third day.

That's not hunger. That's a schedule.

I want the trail quiet, and I want the pelts, because grey stalker is worth real coin at the Crossroads and I am not too proud to say so in the same breath as the rest of it.

They wait on the high ledges.

So look up before you walk under a ridge. Every ridge. It gets tedious and then one day it doesn't.
nb_hillcrest_stalkers.accept_text: On the trail between the hills. Look up before you pass under a ridge.
nb_hillcrest_stalkers.turn_in_text:
Good pelts.

I'll sell what we don't need at the Crossroads. Take this.

nb_serena_bloodfeather.description:
Serena Bloodfeather leads the Witchwings.

She has an old blood-feud with the Horde and a long memory, and I've given up trying to establish which came first.

I have tracked that harpy for years. Years. I know her roosts, her hours, the three ridges she favours in wind and the one she uses in rain.

I have never once gotten close.

And I'll tell you why, because it's the only useful thing I have: she doesn't come at the start of a hunt. She comes at the end, when you've been at it long enough to be tired and pleased with yourself.

She isn't hunting you. She's hunting whoever you are after four hours.

Slayers first. Always.

And if she sees you before you're ready - run to the nearest ridge and fight her there. Don't fight her in the open and don't fight her tired.

You might get close. You'll certainly try, and I've wanted somebody to try for a long time.
nb_serena_bloodfeather.accept_text: The high roosts of the Dry Hills. Slayers first, always.
nb_serena_bloodfeather.turn_in_text:
Serena's dead. The hills are quiet.

I can't believe it. I've said her name every day for six years and now there's nothing on the other end of it.

Take this, with a hunter's thanks.

nb_roost_raiders.description:
Rohna. Earthcaller - I speak with the spirits, which out here mostly means I listen to them complain.

Serena's Hollow is a cliff-gorge that winds up to a harpy roost, and the harpies who live in it don't love visitors.

That's the ordinary part and it isn't why I've asked you here.

The roost is crying out. I can feel it from the mouth of the gorge, through the stone, the way you'd feel a drum two rooms away.

It's a bad cry. Not a threat - pain, or something close enough that I've stopped splitting the difference.

Something up there is wrong and the earth has been carrying it for months.

Go in through the cave mouth.

Bonepickers hold the lower nests. Small, mean, and unreasonably fond of the taste of tauren, which I mention as a warning and not a joke.
nb_roost_raiders.accept_text: In through the cave mouth of Serena's Hollow. The lower nests.
nb_roost_raiders.turn_in_text:
Better. The earth is calmer.

Take this, with the spirits' thanks.

nb_down_from_the_roost.description:
Something practical while you're in there, and then we'll go back to the thing that's actually wrong.

The harpies line their nests with down. Fine, white and warm - warmer than anything we can weave, and I've sat in the smoke of a tauren loom my whole life.

My totem-carvers use it in the rites. Have done since before the roost was anybody's.

There's a symmetry in that which I'd enjoy more under different circumstances.

Pull it out of the nests - handfuls, enough to matter, because a pinch of it does nothing and I'd rather not send you twice.

Mind the sentries. They watch from the high ledges and they're quiet about it.

And I'd like fewer harpies in my sleep, which is the other half of why I'm asking.
nb_down_from_the_roost.accept_text: From the nests in the gorge. Mind the sentries on the high ledges.
nb_down_from_the_roost.turn_in_text:
Soft as a promise.

Thank you. The spirits will be pleased.

Take this.

nb_windcallers_perch.description:
High in the gorge there's a perch, and Windcaller Skreeva stands on it.

She commands the winds that blow the harpies up and down that cliff.

I want you to understand what that means before you go, because it's the whole shape of the place. Nothing in that gorge flies on its own strength. The wind carries them - up to the roost, down to the hunt - and she decides when.

The winds listen to her.

They shouldn't. Wind in a gorge belongs to the gorge, and I've asked it directly and got nothing back but her.

I'd rather they listened to someone else. Anyone else. I'd settle for nobody.

She's on the east ledge, above the middle of the gorge. Her windcallers keep the air thick around her.

Take them first, then her.
nb_windcallers_perch.accept_text: The east ledge, above the middle of the gorge.
nb_windcallers_perch.turn_in_text:
Skreeva's dead. The winds are quiet.

I can hear them breathing again - just breathing, not being told what to do.

Take this.

nb_harpy_matriarch.description:
Top of the gorge. The roost itself - a great bowl of nests, hundreds of them, going back further than anyone's counted.

And in the middle of it, the Matriarch. Mother of every harpy in these hills.

Her cry is the one the earth keeps answering.

That's what I've been hearing since before you came up the gorge, and it's taken me this long to be sure of it - because she isn't calling the harpies and she isn't calling us.

She's calling the ground. Every day. And the ground answers, and I can feel it answering under my feet in the morning before I'm properly awake.

I don't know what she's asking it for and I've decided I don't need to.

End it and this hollow will be quiet.

She won't leave the nest. She'll call every harpy in that roost the moment she sees you.

So don't fight her with the whole flock watching. Thin it first.
nb_harpy_matriarch.accept_text: The roost at the top of the gorge. Don't fight her with the flock watching.
nb_harpy_matriarch.turn_in_text:
The Matriarch's dead. The roost is silent, and the earth with it.

I'll sing the spirits home tonight. It'll be the first time in a year I know they'll hear me.

Take this, and my thanks.
